column5: From BBC Learning English, this is Learning English from the News, our podcast about the news headlines.

column4: In this programme, climate talks fail. What went wrong? Hello, I'm Pippa.
And I'm Becca.
In this programme, we look at one big news story and the vocabulary in the headlines that will help you understand it.
You can find all the vocabulary and headlines from this episode, as well as a free worksheet on our website, bbclearningenglish.com.
So let's hear more about this story.
Countries have failed to reach an agreement to deal with the problem of climate change after disagreements over fossil fuels and money at climate talks in Turkey.
The COP31 talks were the latest in a yearly conference between UN nations to plan and agree commitments and action on climate change.
This was the longest climate conference ever, but the talks collapsed on Sunday after countries were unable to reach an agreement.
Let's have our first headline. This is from the New York Times. U.N. Climate Talks Collapse in a Bitter Clash Over Fossil Fuels.
And that headline, again from the New York Times. U.N. Climate Talks Collapse in a Bitter Clash Over Fossil Fuels.
This headline is about the collapse of the talks and the clash, or disagreement, between countries. We're interested in the description of the clash as bitter.
Bitter literally describes a taste that can be sharp or unpleasant. For example, very strong coffee could be described as bitter. Right.
But we use bitter metaphorically to describe things other than tastes, and then it means unpleasant and involving a lot of anger or unhappiness.
So, for example, my friends recently had a very bitter argument.
They were both very angry with each other, and they didn't speak for a few weeks. In the headline, the clash at the climate talks is described as bitter.
This means it was unpleasant and involved anger and unhappiness from the countries who couldn't agree.
We can also use bitter to describe someone who is angry and unhappy for a long time about something that happened in the past.
For example, the employee was very bitter after the company fired him. He never recovered.
We've had bitter, unpleasant, involving anger or unhappiness.
For example, my friend is in a bitter dispute with his neighbour about some building work. It sounds horrible.
This is Learning English from the News, our podcast about the news headlines. Today we're talking about the failure of important international climate talks.
So, why did the COP31 talks end without an agreement? Well, there are two main reasons.
First, many countries, including EU countries and Pacific island nations were unhappy because the draft agreement didn't include the term fossil fuels.
This is things like oil and gas.
These countries believed an agreement about climate change needed to include a commitment to use fossil fuels less in the future.
The other disagreement was over payments to poorer countries to help them adapt to the impacts of rising temperatures.
Many of these countries wanted the agreement to say exactly how much financial help richer countries would commit to.
Let's have another headline. This is from The Guardian, a UK newspaper.
Cop31 draft climate text dissected: what it says and what it means.
And that headline, again from the Guardian. Cop31 draft climate text dissected: what it says and what it means.
This headline is about the draft agreement at the talks, which countries couldn't agree on. We're interested in this word dissected.
What does it mean to dissect something, Becca?
Well, the verb dissect means separate into smaller parts so that you can look at something in more detail.
You might have dissected an insect or an animal when you were at school.
It involves carefully cutting it up to look at different parts and how they fit together.
We can dissect things like texts too, and that's the meaning in the headline.
It means the writer is going to separate the draft climate agreement into smaller parts to understand what it means.
We use dissect in a similar way to the verb analyse.
And so you might hear it in any situation where someone wants to look in more detail at something.
So, for example, at work you might want to dissect the company's sales results to see what's going well and what's going badly.
And in a more relaxed context.
I call my friend every weekend after our favourite TV show is on, to dissect what happened and what we think might happen next.
We've had dissect, separate into small parts to look at more closely.
For example, the couple went to counselling to dissect what was going wrong in their relationship.
This is Learning English from the News from BBC Learning English. We're talking about the failure of COP31 climate talks.
After the climate talks failed to reach an agreement, a lot of people have been asking what this means for the future of dealing with climate change.
Whilst there wasn't an overall agreement between countries at the conference, experts say progress was made in other areas.
And the failure to reach an agreement doesn't mean climate action stops. Much of it relies on private companies.
But many people believe the failure of the talks means that the way countries work together to act on the climate needs to change.
Previous UN climate talks have led to important agreements, such as the commitment to keep global warming to 1.5C,
but critics say disagreements now will mean action doesn't happen fast enough. Let's have another headline.
This is from New Scientist, a science news magazine. COP31 collapse has shattered the pretence of a global climate consensus.
And that headline, again from New Scientist. COP31 collapse has shattered the pretence of a global climate consensus.
This headline says the failure of the talks has shattered, or broken, the pretence of a global consensus, and consensus means agreement.
We're interested in this word pretence.
Yes, Pippa. Pretence is when a person or a group of people pretend something, when in reality it's not true.
So, in this story, the headline says the talks have broken the pretence of agreement on climate change.
This means that previous climate agreements have made it appear that countries are united on dealing with climate change, but these talks have shown they actually disagree about a lot of things.
We have a couple of common phrases with pretence. We can talk about keeping up a pretence, which means continue pretending something.
For example, the teenager was expelled from school, but he left home in his uniform every morning to keep up the pretence so his parents wouldn't find out.
And the phrase make no pretence means to not pretend anything.
For example, when my sister tells me a boring story, I make no pretence of actually listening to what she says.
We've had pretence, the act of pretending something is true when it's not. For example, you can stop with the pretence.
I know you've organised a surprise birthday party for me. That's it for this episode of Learning English from the News.
We'll be back next week with another news story.
If you're interested in stories about the climate, head to our website where we have a topic page all about the environment and climate change.
It's at bbclearningenglish.com. Bye for now. Bye.",68,2026-11-26T01:58:58Z,https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ssEOLoy8hcw

column6: Come back with me a moment to 2017. You're having a great time because none of us know what a pandemic is.

column4: Comfy mom jeans are back in style, and the Bitcoin you bought back in 2008, it's finally taking off.
(Laughter) You're scrolling on Instagram, and that's pretty cool because they only just started with their algorithmic feed,
so you're still kind of seeing memes and photo dumps from people you actually know.
(Laughter) What's up with all these orange squares?
Influencers and famous faces from Kendall Jenner and Hailey Baldwin, Emily Ratajkowski and Ja Rule are posting about this high-end music festival coming to the Bahamas.
(Laughter) White-sand beaches, luxury accommodations, Migos, Major Lazer, the cultural experience of a decade.
Influencer and celebrity-driven marketing sells out 95 percent of tickets in 48 hours.
Some folks are shelling out up to $100,000 for a spot, and college students are also going for spring break.
Not a bad way to unwind for finals, right? Except it never took place.
Fyre Festival has gone down in history as the greatest party that never happened.
Ticket holders expecting five-star service showed up to bread and cheese sandwiches and FEMA tents.
None of the promised artists performed, and the main organizer ended up in federal prison.
(Laughter) While so much of this was shocking, what really resonated with me was how this was really a story about trust.
A lot of people here were left disappointed. Netflix and Hulu, they got some great fodder.
But hundreds -- no no, thousands of smart, well-off people saw this glamorous, curated content online
and collectively decided this is real, and it’s worth the cost. Humans gravitate to people that we like.
When someone feels relatable, we instinctively trust them more. But relatability and credibility are two very different things.
After years working in legacy newsrooms, I thought I understood how people interact with news to inform our worldviews.
And it wasn't until I later started working also with new-media creators, that I realized just to what extent we are not all dissecting information using the same framework.
Throughout my career in communications, I’ve had this front-row seat to the ways that our evolving media landscape is shaping our democracy,
and the habits journalists use to verify information shouldn't be trade secrets.
They're not difficult or unattainable, but they're not taught outside of newsrooms or journalism schools.
And in today's social media, AI-powered information environment, that skill gap might be the biggest civic problem we have.
Journalists spend years learning a professional discipline of interrogating information in pursuit of the truth.
It's a craft rooted in ethics and moral reasoning.
There's so much that happens inside of a newsroom to ensure accuracy that not everybody realizes, simply because we've never been in that environment.
Facts don't just materialize.
Reporters, editors, fact-checkers and legal teams are all working together to parse out truth.
That looks like gathering information, verifying facts, vetting sources, checking for bias and overall maintaining objectivity to ensure trustworthiness.
We have more access to information than any generation in history. Yet in so many cases, we're thinking less independently than ever before.
Social media and AI algorithms push trending content to the top.
But that doesn't guarantee accuracy, or that we're getting all of the relevant facts that we need to make our own informed opinions.
That disconnect is affecting our media literacy. And it’s happening right when democracy needs [it] most.
The backbone of a strong democracy is in equal parts a free press and an informed, engaged public.
But in the US right now, there are no national media literacy education standards.
It's almost like our media ecosystem has evolved faster than our civic education system.
A kid that's born today won't default to thinking in terms of “The New York Times,” Fox News or PBS.
But they're thinking in terms of Instagram and TikTok and YouTube. 86 percent of Gen Z are turning to social media to get their news.
So when we're living with information bombarding us from the moment we open our eyeballs in the morning,
we all deserve access to the knowledge and techniques journalists use to interpret the world.
Media literacy is what enables us to identify AI, deepfakes and unverified news.
It's also recognizing bias in articles or influencer content that could affect story framing.
It's understanding the role that entertainment plays in broadcast news, and it's unpacking the reasoning behind headlines and visuals.
It's thinking critically about tone and word choice and asking, “How does funding influence this information?”
as well as, ""What's missing from the story and why?"" I'm not saying that journalism is perfect.
Journalists, like all humans, make mistakes, and I'm not saying that AI and social media and influencers should all be left in the dust.

I actually think that traditional newsrooms and new media should learn from one another to ultimately build a faster, more accurate news infrastructure that better meets the needs of today's audience.
The good news is, people all over the world are working on solutions to all of this.
Australia banned social media for kids 16 and under, and Denmark is following their lead.
Germany begins media literacy education in primary school.
Some classrooms will even invite journalists into the class to help teach students how to vet sources,
recognize state-backed disinformation, and also just to pause and take a beat whenever news stokes an emotional reaction before sharing it out.
Finland is another incredible example of standardized media literacy education.
Identifying propaganda and questioning information have been part of Finnish culture ever since the country gained independence from Russia more than a century ago.
So today, media literacy is a core pillar of the national curriculum, beginning K through 12 and carrying through college and adult learning.
Educators in Helsinki have been on CBS and Al Jazeera, describing how media literacy is integrated across all subjects.
So in literature classes, students will learn the basics of verifying news, vetting sources and critiquing media.
Then in math, they'll focus more on algorithms and statistics. In art, they'll take a look at images and learn how they can be edited.

And then in history, it might be taking a look at an air raid that happened during World War II, and considering how it could be taught differently depending [on] which side of the war a country fought on.
Some Finnish students have even played this computer game “Troll Factory,” where they spend a week on this platform,
intentionally acting as an internet troll to spread as much disinformation as they can, with the goal of gaining as much visibility for the account as possible.
One student summed this up as: ""You gain a lot of followers when you spread a lot of unpleasant things.""
Finnish education officials say that the curriculum helps protect democracy, that if we can't tell what's true from what isn't, then we can be deceived and we're left vulnerable.
It roots back to this popular saying, “You have the right to your own opinion, but you do not have the right to your own facts.”
Data shows this standardized approach works.
Finland has ranked at the top of Open Society Foundations' annual Media Literacy Index every year since it started in 2017,
which we all can now recognize as the Orange Square Era here in the US.
I can't help thinking a little bit more about Fyre Festival and wondering how things could have been different
if the folks on those social media teams were asking the same questions that Finnish elementary schoolers ask every day.
And that's where we come in.
We have the power to ask our elected officials to enact national media literacy education standards.
We can practice thinking journalistically in our day-to-day and call out misinformation when we see it -- whether that’s pushing back on something that our friend said
or posting the link to a verified news article on a social media post that is inaccurate.
We can subscribe to our local newspapers, and when we do get our information from social media, we can make sure it's coming from creators who are trained in a journalistic process.
We can share this toolkit with our children and the others in our lives.
So when we leave here today, let’s remember to ask questions -- even with people we tend to agree with.
Let's stay curious, check our sources and speak up in the name of truth, even when it's hard.
Because that ability to think for ourselves might just be the most important civic skill we have left.
Thank you.
